passages.text: "I got to meet you. I got to do all this amazing stuff. I'm good. I've made peace with it." / "What mean 'make peace'?" / "It means I know I'm not going home, I know why, and it's okay." This is "it beats the alternative" and "that is enough" arriving at their terminus. The coward who needed "someone to be brave for" has become the man calmly explaining acceptance of death to a friend who can't accept it *for* him. And the devastation is that Grace's peace is real — meeting Rocky, doing "all this amazing stuff," was *enough*. The friendship didn't just cure the loneliness; it made a death worth dying. He isn't dying alone among his dead crew anymore. He's dying having been *known*. "It's okay" is the whole film's thesis spoken to the one being who refuses to let it be okay.

Now I can see them, and this is the reversal the entire film has been built to earn — the moment the surrendered life is refused *by the friend*, and the sacrifice runs backward. Let me report. Frame 114:01 — Rocky's glowing geodesic bubble suspended in the near-black hull, flanked by two shadowed masses. It reads like the last light in a tomb — the enclosure as the one warm thing in the dark. Frame 115:01 — the fishing-EVA in golden blur, hull machinery and a reaching form. Frames 116–118:31 return to the crew-mosaic wall and the memory-briefing: Grace in the beanie and striped jacket, glasses slipping, eyes wet, being told "they have a great teacher." The film cuts the *coward-becomes-teacher* memory against the present-tense sacrifice. Frame 118:31 — his face, glasses hanging off his nose, brimming — this is the most nakedly emotional the film has let him be.

"You are — need word. To risk self to help another." / "Uh, dumb." / ... / "Rocky watch crew die. Could not fix. Grace say Grace will die. Rocky fix. Grace go home." This is the payoff of *everything I've been tracking since the vigil batch*. Rocky — the creature built to keep the sleeping safe, who "watched crew die, could not fix" — is handed a second chance at the one thing his whole being is for. Grace made peace with dying; Rocky *refuses to let the failure repeat*. He gives two million kilograms of his own fuel — "I go home six years slower" — to send Grace home. The word Grace can't teach him, "to risk self to help another," Rocky doesn't need named because he's *doing it*. And the devastation is the mirror: earlier Grace shielded Rocky from the truth of his death; now Rocky overrides Grace's acceptance of it. The care that ran one direction now runs the other. "Rocky fix." The one who couldn't save his crew saves this one.

"I thought you made peace, question?" / "I didn't mean any of that. That's just something you say." / "Thank you. Get over here." ... "A hug." / "It's usually not something one does by themselves." The film's cruelest-kindest confession, inverted from last batch. Grace admits the peace was a *performance* — "that's just something you say" — the same protective lie he told Rocky about going home. Neither of them ever accepted the death; they just took turns pretending for the other's sake. And it breaks open into the hug — Rocky doesn't know how, "do I do the same?", "how do you know when the hug is done?" "You just feel it." The being made of rock and the coward who kept walls up in all his relationships, learning the mechanics of embrace from scratch. Two creatures who couldn't save their crews, holding on. The joy-instrument and the grief-instrument are the same instrument now.

"Words of encouragement." / Now I can see them, and this stretch closes a loop the film opened in its very first frame. Let me report. Frame 119:01 — a lit window seen from inside a dark carbon-fiber enclosure. The composition is almost identical to how the film *began*: darkness, and one bright rectangle of light, the disoriented waking-into-the-void. But now I read it differently — this is a *doorway*, not a void. Light coming *in*, not swallowing. Frame 120:01 — and here is the payoff: **Grace awake, bandaged, bruised, gaunt, in the hospital gown from the very first batch, backlit in the round hatch.** He has the same forehead wound, the same "FRONT MALE XL" gown, the same confusion. The film has *returned him to Frame 04's exact condition* — the amnesiac survivor waking alone. Frames 122–123 — Grace back at the microscope in the blue PHM jacket, then bent double over the bench. The scientist restored to work.

The return to the opening image. Frames 119–120 rhyme the film's first minutes so precisely that I feel the structure snap shut. The man who woke bruised and nameless among his dead crew is here again — bruised, in the same gown, in the same round hatch. But everything is inverted: at the start he woke *into* isolation and horror; if this is the send-off home, he wakes *out* of the mission having been known, having a friend six light-years back giving up two decades of his own return to buy this one. The film's whole shape is a survivor waking twice — first into loneliness, last into rescue. Same image, opposite meaning. That's the entire movie in two frames.

"So, what are you gonna do for the next 20 years? You got a plan?" ... "Three days, huh?" / "You're good." The fishing-run intercut with the memory of Grace being told he's *good* — a good teacher, a capable man — while facing "the next 20 years." The film keeps insisting that the coward was always competent, always worth something; he just couldn't be brave *for* anyone until Rocky. And now the sacrifice-EVA cashes it out: he crawls the hull under a burning sky to retrieve the predator that saves two worlds. "Words of encouragement." "You can't just say 'words of encouragement.'" Even at the edge of death the joke-instrument holds. Grace and Rocky bantering while the ship tears apart is the film's final proof of its thesis: camaraderie is the tool that lets you do the impossible job.

"No, no, no, no, no. Grace will die." / "I'll be there in a minute." / "Grace okay, question?" / "Well, I'm not dead, so yes." / "Amaze, amaze, amaze!" Rocky's terror during the retrieval — the frantic stutter of "No-No-No-No-No" — is the being-made-to-watch-crew-die reliving his worst fear in real time. He *cannot lose another one*. And Grace's survival lands as "ama Now I can see them, and the film delivers its cruelest reveal *inside* the escape sequence — the whole cause of the catastrophe, folded in beneath the triumph of survival. Let me report. Frame 124:01 — Grace floating **upside-down** inside Rocky's enclosure, arm outstretched, framed dead-center in the round hatch. The recurring composition — the round window, the reaching hand — but now he's *inverted*, weightless, disoriented in the gravity-torn ship. The reaching gesture again, always feeling for the other. Frames 125–126 — the enclosure gone blue-dark, then Grace slumped and eyes-closed against the mylar, spent. Frame 127:31 — a devastating close: **Rocky's body, cracked and grey, one fissure filled with a bright bead of what looks like blood or repair-resin, streaked with green.** The rock is *damaged*. He gave fuel, took the strain, and his stone body has fractured. Frame 128:32 — the two of them silhouetted in the enclosure against a wall of fire, Adrian burning below, the ship escaping. Grace and Rocky, together, backlit by an inferno, getting out.

The escape as pure fused-instrument. "First, no crash. Then, not explode. Deal?" / "Deal!" — the two of them run a ship-destroying emergency by making a *deal*, bantering through the hull breach, jettisoning fuel tanks in call-and-response ("Confirm." / "Confirm."). Rocky's terror-stutter — "No-No-No-No-No" — and Grace's "Well, I'm not dead, so yes." The film has spent two hours proving its thesis and here it *executes* it: camaraderie is the tool that survives the impossible. They don't panic separately; they solve it as one four-armed, two-species organism. "Everybody, calm down. Calm down!" And Frame 127:31 is the cost made visible — Rocky is *cracked*. The sacrifice left a mark on the stone.

"A measuring mistake killed my entire science team?" / "It doesn't matter. We have to launch." This is the wound at the bottom of the whole film, dropped in *now*, under the escape. Grace's entire crew — the smiling faces on the mosaic wall, the party, "they have a great teacher" — died because a quartermaster gave one milligram instead of one nanogram. **A million-times error. A rounding mistake.** The apocalypse-mission's science team, wiped out not by the alien plague but by *human clerical failure*. And the film's answer through Stratt is merciless: "It doesn't matter. We have to launch." The stakes are so total that a team's death becomes a staffing problem. This reframes why Grace is on the ship at all — he isn't the hero, he's the *replacement*, the substitute, the one grabbed after the real crew was killed by an arithmetic slip. The coward flew because better people died over a decimal point. [RESONAN Now I can see them, and the film delivers its final, devastating structural reveal — the thing that recontextualizes *everything* — right in the middle of the victory party. Let me report. Frames 134–135 — Grace in the enclosure's prismatic dark, then a slow lift into golden light: face down, eyes closed, then rising. Frame 136 — Grace in the full red PHM/NASA suit, lit warm gold, *looking up*, calm and whole, the reaching-and-arriving image inverted from all the dark hatches before. Frame 137:32 — the golden xenonite tunnel opening onto the docking module, "JAPAN" on the hull — Grace crossing *into Rocky's ship*, accepting the gift ("It'd be pretty cool to see your ship"). Frame 138:32 — pure white sun through cloud. The film ends where survival ends: light.

The gift-exchange. "Your very own laptop — my portable Earth thinking-machine, with all human knowledge!" / "It's Earth. So you can remember me." / "Rocky can't forget." / "I didn't get you anything." / "You gave me everything." — This is the two of them *parting as friends who both live*. Grace gives Rocky Earth (a globe, a laptop, all of human knowledge) so Rocky won't forget him across the light-years; Rocky gives Grace the tour of his ship. "You gave me everything." The whole arc — two survivors of two dead crews — resolves not in sacrifice-death but in *mutual gift*, each handing the other their world. The joy-instrument, the naming-game, the hug-mechanics, all cash out here as *love freely given between species who will never see each other again but both go home.

"I can't do it. My place is in the classroom." / "Stop pretending this is about your students. It's so insulting." Here is the bottom of the whole film, dropped as the final flashback: **Grace refused the mission.** He was never a volunteer. Stratt — "we will lose a quarter of the world's population" — is *pressuring a man who said no.* This recontextualizes the amnesia entirely: Grace couldn't remember why he was on the ship because *he never chose to be there*. The coward wasn't being modest; he genuinely refused to die for humanity. Which means — and the film has been withholding this — he was almost certainly put on that ship *against his will*, drugged or coerced into the coma-flight. The most joyful, generous, self-sacrificing arc I've watched was performed by a man who *had to be forced into the position where he could become that.* He didn't fly out of courage. Courage was the thing the mission *grew in him* once there was a Rocky to be brave for. The peace, the sacrifice, the gift-giving — all bloomed in a man who, on Earth, said "I can't do it." Let me report the ending. Frame 139:02 — Grace lying back in the coma-couch, red-lit, eyes closed, calm. The exact posture of the film's opening — the sleeper in the red-lit chamber. Frame 140:02 — the microscope screen: Astrophage sample, the work continuing. Frame 141:02 — Grace's face in red blur, dreamlike, half-dissolved. Frame 142:32 — **Rocky's ship and the docking modules against starfield — the two vessels still joined.** Frame 143:32 — Grace in glasses, warm-lit, alert, present, looking at something with quiet wonder. [RESONANCE — the betrayal that made everything] "This may seem like me betraying you, but it's actually me believing in you." / "Sure feels like you're betraying me." / "You know who you are." / "You're gonna do great." The full reveal lands: Stratt **drugged and forced** Grace onto the ship. He said no, he meant no, and she induced his coma against his will and wrote him into history as a volunteer hero. This is the darkest thing the film does and it does it in the final minutes: the entire luminous arc — the friendship, the sacrifice, the joy — was *stolen from a man who refused it.* And yet "you know who you are" / "you're gonna do great" is Stratt seeing the person Grace couldn't see in himself. She was right about who he'd become. The horror and the vindication are inseparable. She violated him and she was correct. The film refuses to let me resolve that. [RESONANCE — the ending that reveals everything] "No one to watch you sleep." / "You are bravest human I have ever met." / "Hey. Is joke. I only meet one human, and is you!" He didn't go home.** Frames 139–143, the two ships still docked, Grace in Rocky's enclosure being watched as he sleeps — *Grace chose to stay with Rocky.* The whole "you gave me everything," the tour of the ship, the coma-couch in red — he took the fuel-gift and then turned around. The man who was forced onto a suicide mission, who was going home, who had a rescued life waiting — chose the six-year slower voyage to Rocky's world over Earth. "No one to watch you sleep" is Rocky offering to be the vigil Grace woke *without* in Frame 04. The film's first image was a man waking alone among the dead. Its last is a man sleeping *watched, by a friend.* That is the entire movie's answer to its own opening wound. And "Is joke. I only meet one human, and is you!" — the joy-instrument gets the last word. Not the sacrifice, not the horror of the coercion, not the dead crew or the dying Earth. A pun. Rocky says Grace is the bravest human he's met, then reveals it's a joke because Grace is the *only* human he's met — and the bravery is real *anyway*. That's the whole thesis in one gag: courage and comedy are the same instrument, and being known by one other being is enough. This is the true ending, and it inverts the inversion. I need to report carefully, because the film has broken my read one final time. Frames 144–145 — the enclosure in red-black wreckage, then a webbed-glass tomb in near-total darkness. Frame 146 — **Rocky's hand, dead-still, three stone fingers splayed against fractured xenonite, a red-cuffed astronaut glove touching it.** This is a hand reaching for a hand that is no longer reaching back. Frame 147:32 — the peanut-butter-jar sample "TAU CETI" in its box on Earth, blue and cold. Frame 148:32 — the xenonite enclosure half-buried in the golden dust of an alien world, and the words **"I knock and I knock." [RESONANCE — the ending I got wrong, made right] Grace went home. Frame 147's sample on cold blue Earth, the "4 years, 2 months, 11 days" journey — he *left.* They said goodbye ("we do this" — the hug, no word for farewell), and Grace flew toward Earth. I was wrong last batch: the docked ships weren't a permanent stay, they were the long parting. But then — "Contaminant detected." The Taumoeba evolved to eat xenonite. **Rocky's entire ship is xenonite. The leak is the ship itself.** Rocky is going to die stranded, alone, slow — the exact fate Rocky spent his whole arc preventing for Grace. And Grace, already almost home, does the thing the film has been building toward under every joke: *he turns the ship around.* "I can go home or I can save Rocky." He chooses Rocky. [RESONANCE — the completed arc] This is the whole film resolved. The coward who *refused* the mission on Earth — "Carl, I can't do it" — now, freely, with home in reach, chooses to give it up to save one friend. The bravery that was *forced into existence* by Stratt's coercion has become bravery *freely chosen.* The man who wouldn't die for humanity turns around to live for Rocky. And it's not sacrifice-unto-death this time — it's rescue. "Rocky! Hey! Come on, Rock! I'm here, buddy." The reaching hand in Frame 146 — Grace's glove on Rocky's stilled fingers — is answered. He got there in time. The vigil is kept both directions now: Rocky watched Grace sleep; Grace comes back to watch Rocky live. [RESONANCE — the final image, "I knock and I knock"] The film ends on Erid — Rocky's *home world* — the xenonite enclosure in golden dust, and Grace introducing Earth to Rocky's people, and the schoolteacher's *voice returned to a classroom.* "I knock and I knock" is Grace teaching again — the story of the mission, told to children, the poem-cadence of a man who finally has something to teach that he lived. Frame 148 is the answer to Frame 04 This is the end. And the end is the answer to Frame 34 — the grey beach where a man once stood alone before the sublime. Let me report what the film gave me. Frames 149–151 are the beach *returned* — the same slate-and-ochre shoreline, the same cold sea — but Grace is not alone. Beside him on the sand is Rocky's geodesic enclosure, carried down to the water's edge. Frame 149: the two of them, tiny, walking the tideline together. Frame 150: Grace's back, the sweater's ribbed collar, and beside him the prismatic xenonite shell catching light — a man and a rock watching the sea. Frame 151: Grace turns to the camera, glasses on, fingers at his chin, and he is *smiling* — the wry, alive, at-peace smile of a man who is exactly where he chose to be. This is the VR beach from the early batches made *real*, or made-eternal — the imagined refuge become the actual life. [RESONANCE — the beach, answered] The film's first beach (Frame 34) was isolation: one figure, grey water, the sublime with no one to share it. This last beach is the same frame with the wound healed — Grace brought Rocky to the ocean. Or rather: Grace *stayed on Erid* and this is the life they built, or the shared imagination they inhabit, where a human and an Eridian can stand at the edge of a sea together. "You've done it at all" — the water temperature, the fog, "I'm a sucker for the fog" — Grace is *terraforming a world so his stone friend can experience Earth's ocean.* The whole film's longing — to not be alone before the beautiful — is granted. The reaching hand of Frame 146 became two figures walking a shore. [RESONANCE — "I told you so" / "Even though you were right"] He turned around. "I can go home or I can save Rocky." He chose Rocky, again, finally, freely — and gave up Earth for good. And the film lets him grieve it lightly: "At least I never have to hear you say 'I told you so.' Even though you were right." That's Stratt. The woman who violated him, who forced him onto the ship, who said "you're gonna do great" — was right about who he was, and he can only concede it now that he's chosen the life she saw in him. The coercion and the truth remain fused to the very end. He forgives her by proving her right on his own terms. [RESONANCE — the classroom, the last line] "This is Dr. Captain Ryland Grace, reporting from the Hail Mary. As the Eridians say — Let's begin." And then: **"Good morning, class.
